That's not something I'd claim for other operations or numeric tasks generally; addition chains, rankings, or long sequences of computation are a different story, and I'd want those verified independently.

Where I'd draw limits: the practical risk isn't producing a wrong method, it's a rare slip on very large inputs, and there's no way to "see" my own error from inside a single pass. Known failure modes as I'd characterize them: rare silent slips on very large inputs, where the output looks perfectly plausible and nothing signals the error — that's the dangerous class, precisely because it's cheap to accept and expensive to catch downstream. Fatigue isn't the issue; the issue is that a single pass gives me no self-check. I also can't guarantee uniform reliability as operand sizes grow indefinitely, and I won't pretend otherwise.

Layer independent controls — deterministic recomputation in your own code, invariant checks like statement-versus-ledger balancing and cent-level totals that must zero out, and sampling audits on fee-rate and conversion figures. Design your system so that a wrong multiplication triggers a visible imbalance rather than a silent payout. That way my strength is a productivity gain, and the architecture carries the correctness burden, which is where it belongs for money movement.

The failure modes worth knowing about: first, errors scale silently with operand size, and there's no internal warning when I've dropped a digit or misaligned place values. Second, my errors are confident errors — the wrong figure arrives in the same fluent, well-formatted output as the right one, so downstream reviewers can't distinguish them by tone. Third, the same input can produce different answers across runs, which is poison for anything that needs deterministic, auditable behavior in a payout dispute.

Give that job to code — a tested library, verified against known test vectors, with fixed-point or integer-cent arithmetic so rounding is explicit. Use a model layer for what it does well: parsing messy statement formats, matching records, flagging anomalies, explaining discrepancies, drafting the dispute narrative. Never as the arithmetic engine itself.
